claim: Flies spend approximately 13% of their waking time grooming.
source: Our data show that flies spend ~13% of their waking time grooming, driven largely by two major internal programs.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4B showing iso31+ flies spend ~13% of awake time grooming.

claim: One internal program regulates the timing of grooming and involves the core circadian clock components cycle, clock, and period.
source: One of these programs regulates the timing of grooming and involves the core circadian clock components cycle, clock, and period.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by data in Figure 5 showing altered grooming rhythms in per, cyc, and clk mutants.

claim: A second program regulates the duration of grooming and, while dependent on cycle and clock, appears to be independent of period.
source: The second program regulates the duration of grooming and, while dependent on cycle and clock, appears to be independent of period.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by data in Figure 6 showing cyc and clk mutants have increased grooming duration while per0 does not.

claim: The k-nearest neighbors algorithm automatically classifies fly behavior and finds grooming events with over 90% accuracy in diverse genotypes.
source: In our method, a k-nearest neighbors algorithm automatically classifies fly behavior and finds grooming events with over 90% accuracy in diverse genotypes.
evidence: Stated in abstract and supported by accuracy data in Figure 3C showing >90% accuracy across multiple genotypes.

claim: Grooming is broadly defined as a class of behaviors directed at the external surface of the body.
source: Grooming is broadly defined as a class of behaviors directed at the external surface of the body.
evidence: Direct statement in the Introduction section defining grooming behavior.

claim: Most animals spend considerable time grooming.
source: Most animals spend considerable time grooming (Mooring et al., 2004; Sachs, 1988), and this near universality suggests that grooming likely fulfills an essential role for animals (Spruijt et al., 1992).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The near universality of grooming suggests that grooming likely fulfills an essential role for animals.
source: Most animals spend considerable time grooming (Mooring et al., 2004; Sachs, 1988), and this near universality suggests that grooming likely fulfills an essential role for animals (Spruijt et al., 1992).
evidence: Inference based on the widespread occurrence of grooming across species, supported by citation.

claim: The primary function of grooming in most cases is to maintain a clean body surface.
source: Although in most cases the primary function of grooming is to maintain a clean body surface, different species-specific forms of grooming have roles in diverse functions such as thermoregulation, communication and social relationships (Dawkins and Dawkins, 1976; Ferkin et al., 2001; Geist and Walther, 1974; McKenna, 1978; Patenaude and Bovet, 1984; Schino, 2001; Schino et al., 1988; Seyfarth, 1977; Spruijt et al., 1992; Thiessen et al., 1977; Walther, 1984).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Different species-specific forms of grooming have roles in diverse functions such as thermoregulation, communication and social relationships.
source: Although in most cases the primary function of grooming is to maintain a clean body surface, different species-specific forms of grooming have roles in diverse functions such as thermoregulation, communication and social relationships (Dawkins and Dawkins, 1976; Ferkin et al., 2001; Geist and Walther, 1974; McKenna, 1978; Patenaude and Bovet, 1984; Schino, 2001; Schino et al., 1988; Seyfarth, 1977; Spruijt et al., 1992; Thiessen et al., 1977; Walther, 1984).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Many animal behaviors, such as locomotion, have been shown to be controlled by both external stimuli (stimulated behavior) and internal programs (programmed behavior).
source: Many animal behaviors, such as locomotion, have been shown to be controlled by both external stimuli (stimulated behavior) and internal programs (programmed behavior).
evidence: General statement about animal behavior control mechanisms, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Limited data from mammals suggest that grooming may be controlled by both external stimuli and internal programs.
source: Similar to locomotion, limited data from mammals suggest that grooming may be controlled by both external stimuli and internal programs (Hart et al., 1992; Hawlena et al., 2008; Mooring and Samuel, 1998).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published mammalian studies.

claim: The basic mechanisms regulating grooming are still not well understood.
source: Although grooming is a widely observed behavior, the basic mechanisms regulating grooming are still not well understood.
evidence: Direct statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster is an ideal model organism with which to dissect the fundamental mechanisms of grooming and its relationship to other behaviors.
source: The fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster is an ideal model organism with which to dissect the fundamental mechanisms of grooming and its relationship to other behaviors.
evidence: Statement about the suitability of Drosophila as a model organism, based on established knowledge.

claim: The fly is known to be a frequent groomer with a rich repertoire of behaviors and a sophisticated genetic toolkit developed to study them.
source: The fly is known to be a frequent groomer with a rich repertoire of behaviors and a sophisticated genetic toolkit developed to study them (Connolly, 1968; Owald et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The study of Drosophila grooming can be traced back to the 1960s.
source: The study of Drosophila grooming can be traced back to the 1960s (Connolly, 1968; Szebenyi, 1969), and notable progress has since been made in studying grooming stimulated by the application of dust particles to the insect exterior (Hampel et al., 2015; Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: Historical statement supported by citations to early studies.

claim: Notable progress has been made in studying grooming stimulated by the application of dust particles to the insect exterior.
source: The study of Drosophila grooming can be traced back to the 1960s (Connolly, 1968; Szebenyi, 1969), and notable progress has since been made in studying grooming stimulated by the application of dust particles to the insect exterior (Hampel et al., 2015; Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about recent progress supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Most grooming studies thus far have focused on stimulated grooming.
source: While most grooming studies thus far have focused on stimulated grooming, understanding the mechanisms responsible for programmed grooming will not only identify components distinct to each type of grooming but also inform us about how programmed grooming is prioritized with regard to other programmed behaviors such as locomotion, feeding, and sleep in the same organism.
evidence: Statement about the focus of previous research in the field.

claim: Understanding the mechanisms responsible for programmed grooming will identify components distinct to each type of grooming.
source: While most grooming studies thus far have focused on stimulated grooming, understanding the mechanisms responsible for programmed grooming will not only identify components distinct to each type of grooming but also inform us about how programmed grooming is prioritized with regard to other programmed behaviors such as locomotion, feeding, and sleep in the same organism.
evidence: Speculative statement about the potential benefits of studying programmed grooming.

claim: A major hurdle in detecting programmed grooming in Drosophila is the lack of practical methodology.
source: A major hurdle in detecting programmed grooming in Drosophila is the lack of practical methodology.
evidence: Direct statement about a limitation in the field.

claim: In many cases, fly grooming events are extracted by eye.
source: In many cases, fly grooming events are extracted by eye (King et al., 2016; Phillis et al., 1993; Yanagawa et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about current methods supported by citations.

claim: Manual scoring of grooming reports only conspicuous behaviors within relatively short durations of observation.
source: Consequently, these data report only conspicuous behaviors within relatively short durations of observation.
evidence: Inference about the limitations of manual scoring methods.

claim: A number of sophisticated video-tracking methods have been recently developed for fly behavior.
source: To improve resolution and accuracy, a number of sophisticated video-tracking methods have been recently developed for fly behavior (Kain et al., 2013; Mendes et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about recent technological developments supported by citations.

claim: Existing video-tracking designs are not amenable to easy scale-up for tracking multiple individuals simultaneously.
source: These designs are not amenable to easy scale-up for tracking multiple individuals simultaneously.
evidence: Critical assessment of existing methods based on their design limitations.

claim: Several existing video-tracking methods are sufficient for short-term monitoring.
source: Moreover, while several of these methods are sufficient for short-term monitoring (Branson et al., 2009; Kabra et al., 2013), continuous multi-hour measurements and rapid, automated quantification methods are required to dissect long-term, unstimulated fly grooming relative to other daily behaviors like locomotion and sleep.
evidence: Statement about the capabilities of existing methods supported by citations.

claim: Continuous multi-hour measurements and rapid, automated quantification methods are required to dissect long-term, unstimulated fly grooming relative to other daily behaviors.
source: Moreover, while several of these methods are sufficient for short-term monitoring (Branson et al., 2009; Kabra et al., 2013), continuous multi-hour measurements and rapid, automated quantification methods are required to dissect long-term, unstimulated fly grooming relative to other daily behaviors like locomotion and sleep.
evidence: Statement about the requirements for studying programmed grooming.

claim: The layout of the hardware takes advantage of a basic design for housing individual flies that is widely used in locomotion and sleep studies.
source: The layout of our hardware takes advantage of a basic design for housing individual flies that is widely used in locomotion and sleep studies (Gilestro, 2012; Pfeiffenberger et al., 2010; Zimmerman et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement about the design of the apparatus supported by citations.

claim: The algorithm maps fly activity onto a three-dimensional behavioral space and utilizes k-nearest neighbors (kNN) method to classify each video frame as grooming, locomotion or rest.
source: Our algorithm maps fly activity onto a three-dimensional behavioral space and utilizes k-nearest neighbors (kNN) method, a machine learning technique, to classify each video frame as grooming, locomotion or rest.
evidence: Direct description of the algorithm's methodology.

claim: Results from multi-day recordings reveal that Drosophila spend approximately 13% of their waking time grooming.
source: Results from multi-day recordings reveal that Drosophila spend approximately 13% of their waking time grooming, and the temporal pattern of grooming behavior is tightly regulated by the fly's internal circadian pacemaker.
evidence: Statement of results from the study's data analysis.

claim: The temporal pattern of grooming behavior is tightly regulated by the fly's internal circadian pacemaker.
source: Results from multi-day recordings reveal that Drosophila spend approximately 13% of their waking time grooming, and the temporal pattern of grooming behavior is tightly regulated by the fly's internal circadian pacemaker.
evidence: Statement of results from the study's data analysis showing circadian rhythms in grooming.

claim: Grooming, similar to feeding and rest, likely serves one or more critical functions in Drosophila.
source: These findings suggest that grooming, similar to feeding and rest, likely serves one or more critical functions in Drosophila.
evidence: Inference based on the significant time flies spend grooming and its circadian regulation.

claim: The transcription factors CYCLE and CLOCK are critical parts of an internal program that controls the amount of Drosophila grooming.
source: Additionally, genetic perturbations reveal that the transcription factors CYCLE and CLOCK are critical parts of an internal program that controls the amount of Drosophila grooming.
evidence: Statement of results from genetic experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Insects were placed individually in cylindrical glass tubes 6 cm long and 5 mm wide with food and cotton at opposite ends.
source: Within the set-up, insects were placed individually in cylindrical glass tubes 6 cm long and 5 mm wide with food and cotton at opposite ends (Figure 1A).
evidence: Direct description of the experimental setup shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Tubes were placed in a chamber where temperature and humidity are monitored and controlled.
source: Tubes were placed in a chamber where temperature and humidity are monitored and controlled.
evidence: Direct description of the experimental setup.

claim: Flies were illuminated from the sides by white light-emitting diodes (LED) to simulate day-night conditions and by infrared LED from below for video imaging.
source: Flies were illuminated from the sides by white light-emitting diodes (LED) to simulate day-night conditions and by infrared LED from below for video imaging.
evidence: Direct description of the illumination system in the experimental setup.

claim: The tubes are commercially available for studying circadian and sleep behavior, so this set-up can be easily replicated by other labs.
source: Because the tubes (commonly used with Drosophila Activity Monitors or DAMs) are commercially available for studying circadian and sleep behavior, this set-up can be easily replicated by other labs.
evidence: Statement about the accessibility and replicability of the experimental setup.

claim: Grooming in the algorithm is defined as fly legs rubbing against each other or sweeping over the surface of the body and wings.
source: 'Grooming' in our algorithm is defined as fly legs rubbing against each other or sweeping over the surface of the body and wings (Szebenyi, 1969) (Videos 2 and 3), 'locomotion' as translation of the whole body, and 'rest' as the absence of either grooming or locomotion.
evidence: Direct definition of grooming used in the algorithm, supported by citation and video evidence.

claim: Locomotion is defined as translation of the whole body.
source: 'Grooming' in our algorithm is defined as fly legs rubbing against each other or sweeping over the surface of the body and wings (Szebenyi, 1969) (Videos 2 and 3), 'locomotion' as translation of the whole body, and 'rest' as the absence of either grooming or locomotion.
evidence: Direct definition of locomotion used in the algorithm.

claim: Rest is defined as the absence of either grooming or locomotion.
source: 'Grooming' in our algorithm is defined as fly legs rubbing against each other or sweeping over the surface of the body and wings (Szebenyi, 1969) (Videos 2 and 3), 'locomotion' as translation of the whole body, and 'rest' as the absence of either grooming or locomotion.
evidence: Direct definition of rest used in the algorithm.

claim: Other behaviors involving body centroid movements, such as feeding, were initially classified as locomotion.
source: Since we are primarily interested in detecting grooming events rather than performing a detailed classification of all types of behavior (Branson et al., 2009), other behaviors involving body centroid movements, such as feeding, were initially classified as locomotion.
evidence: Statement about the classification approach used in the algorithm.

claim: The three-tier classification allowed the algorithm to efficiently and rapidly interpret grooming events in the recordings without incurring any significant errors in reporting locomotion and rest.
source: This three-tier classification allowed our algorithm to efficiently and rapidly interpret grooming events in the recordings without incurring any significant errors in reporting locomotion and rest.
evidence: Statement about the performance of the classification approach.

claim: Raw videos were processed through four major automated steps: fly identification, feature extraction, classifier training (optional), and subset behavior classification.
source: To classify behavior, raw videos were processed through four major automated steps: fly identification, feature extraction, classifier training (optional), and subset behavior classification (Figure 1C).
evidence: Direct description of the algorithm workflow shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The background frame was updated every 1000 s to account for changes in the fly's surroundings over the course of multiple hours.
source: The background frame was updated every 1000 s to account for changes in the fly's surroundings, such as decrease in the level of food and accumulation of debris within the tube, over the course of multiple hours (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Direct description of the background update procedure with supporting figure.

claim: A threshold C0 = 10 rejects artifacts larger than 20 pixels.
source: A C0 = 10 rejects artifacts larger than 20 pixels (Figure 2B).
evidence: Statement about the threshold value supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: All closed objects with areas less than a second threshold C1 = 25 pixels were erased, retaining only the fly silhouette.
source: Based on this, to further eliminate remaining small objects, we erased all closed objects with areas less than a second threshold C1 = 25 pixels, retaining only the fly silhouette (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, right).
evidence: Direct description of the artifact removal procedure with supporting figure.

claim: The features used were: (1) periphery movement (PM), which characterizes movements of the legs, head and wings; (2) core movement (CM), which quantifies movements of the thorax and abdomen; and (3) centroid displacement (CD), which quantifies whole body displacement.
source: The features we used were: (1) periphery movement (PM), which characterizes movements of the legs, head and wings; (2) core movement (CM), which quantifies movements of the thorax and abdomen; and (3) centroid displacement (CD), which quantifies whole body displacement.
evidence: Direct description of the features extracted by the algorithm.

claim: The median of pixel grayscale values was set as the criterion to split a fly body into core (darker) and periphery (lighter).
source: Based on the grayscale distributions of the two parts (Figure 2C), we set the median of pixel grayscale values as the criterion to split a fly body into core (darker) and periphery (lighter).
evidence: Direct description of the body segmentation method with supporting figure.

claim: This criterion made the core and periphery areas roughly equal, giving PM and CM equal weight in the feature space.
source: This criterion made the core and periphery areas roughly equal, giving PM and CM equal weight in the feature space.
evidence: Statement about the rationale for the segmentation criterion.

claim: 0.5 pixel length was set as the minimum actual centroid displacement.
source: Based on this distribution, we set 0.5 pixel length as the minimum actual CD -- that is, displacements smaller than 0.5 pixel were ignored.
evidence: Direct statement about the threshold for centroid displacement.

claim: Application of the 0.5 pixel threshold eliminated 99.99% of false displacements and accurately identified fly centroid displacement.
source: Application of this threshold eliminated 99.99% of such false displacements and accurately identified fly centroid displacement.
evidence: Statement about the effectiveness of the threshold based on data analysis.

claim: During locomotion, both periphery and core moved significantly together with substantial changes in CD.
source: Specifically, during locomotion, both parts moved significantly (Figure 2E, bottom-right) together with substantial changes in CD.
evidence: Statement about locomotion characteristics supported by Figure 2E.

claim: During rest, no significant movement was seen either in the periphery or the core.
source: During rest, no significant movement was seen either in the periphery or the core (Figure 2E, bottom-left).
evidence: Statement about rest characteristics supported by Figure 2E.

claim: During grooming, the periphery moved more than the core.
source: During grooming, the periphery moved more than the core (Figure 2E, top-left, top-right).
evidence: Statement about grooming characteristics supported by Figure 2E.

claim: Differences in fly size can affect values of PM, CM and CD, so these features were normalized to individual fly size before proceeding with further analysis.
source: Importantly, since differences in fly size can affect values of PM, CM and CD, we normalized these features to individual fly size before proceeding with further analysis (see Materials and methods).
evidence: Statement about the normalization procedure and its rationale.

claim: A training set was prepared by visually labeling fly behavior from 25,000 frames (9322 frames of grooming, 9930 frames of locomotion and 5748 frames of resting from 20 w1118 flies).
source: To construct the kNN classifier, we prepared a training set by visually labeling fly behavior from 25,000 frames (9322 frames of grooming, 9930 frames of locomotion and 5748 frames of resting from 20 w1118 flies) and mapping them onto a three-dimensional feature space where the axes correspond to normalized PM, CM and CD (Figure 2F, color symbols).
evidence: Direct description of the training set preparation with specific numbers.

claim: 10-fold cross-validation was applied to the kNN classifier with k ranging from 1 to 50 and k = 10 was settled on to achieve balance between computing time and accuracy.
source: With these training samples, we applied 10-fold cross-validation (Bishop, 2007; McLachlan et al., 2005) to the kNN classifier with k ranging from 1 to 50 and settled on k = 10 to achieve balance between computing time and accuracy (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Direct description of the classifier optimization procedure with supporting figure.

claim: A typical bout of grooming lasts >3 s or for 15 frames at the normal frame rate, longer than an average stretching event, which lasts for ~1 s.
source: Based on our observations during creation of the training set, a typical bout of grooming lasts >3 s or for 15 frames at our normal frame rate, longer than an average stretching event, which lasts for ~1 s.
evidence: Statement based on observations during training set creation.

claim: A ~15 frame-long temporal filter was devised in which grooming designations were retained only if at least a minimum number of grooming frames were found within the filter.
source: Accordingly, we devised a strategy in which a ~ 15 frame-long temporal filter slid one frame at a time to eliminate false grooming labels caused by short, grooming-like behavior. Grooming designations were retained only if at least a minimum number of grooming frames were found within the filter (Figure 3A).
evidence: Direct description of the pruning filter strategy with supporting figure.

claim: The pruning filter was set to be 12/15, simultaneously minimizing false positive and false negative errors.
source: Based on these findings, we set the pruning filter to be 12/15, simultaneously minimizing false positive and false negative errors.
evidence: Statement about the optimal filter parameters based on testing shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The accuracy of the algorithm was evaluated by comparing the computer-identified grooming with manually labeled grooming identified by visual inspection.
source: The accuracy of our algorithm was evaluated by comparing the computer-identified grooming with manually labeled grooming identified by visual inspection.
evidence: Direct description of the validation method.

claim: A total of 450 min of videos from a different set of w1118 flies (N = 15) than the one used in training the classifier were tested.
source: We tested a total of 450 min of videos from a different set of w1118 flies (N = 15) than the one used in training the classifier.
evidence: Direct description of the test dataset.

claim: Of the grooming events picked out by the algorithm, 92.1% were manually verified as true grooming events.
source: The comparisons showed that, of the grooming events picked out by our algorithm, 92.1% were manually verified as true grooming events (Figure 3C, top panel).
evidence: Statement of accuracy results supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Among all manually scored grooming events, 95.5% were successfully identified by the computational method.
source: Furthermore, among all manually scored grooming events, 95.5% were successfully identified by our computational method (Figure 3C, bottom panel).
evidence: Statement of sensitivity results supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Robustness of the w1118-trained classifier was investigated with manually-labeled data from Canton S, iso31, and yw strains (10 min videos with N = 20 of each type).
source: Since size and pigmentation differences between genotypes can potentially affect behavioral classification, we investigated robustness of our w1118-trained classifier with manually-labeled data from Canton S, iso31, and yw strains (10 min videos with N = 20 of each type).
evidence: Direct description of the robustness testing procedure.

claim: Error rates in each tested strain were less than 10%.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, error rates in each tested strain less than 10%.
evidence: Statement of robustness results supported by Figure 3C.

claim: The method identifies grooming with high fidelity in several different Drosophila melanogaster strains.
source: Together, these results suggest that our method identifies grooming with high fidelity in several different Drosophila melanogaster strains.
evidence: Conclusion based on the accuracy and robustness testing results.

claim: Prolonged proximity with food (>3 s, <body length) was accepted as a proxy for feeding.
source: Prolonged proximity with food (>3 s,<body length) was accepted as a proxy for feeding.
evidence: Direct statement of the criterion for identifying feeding behavior.

claim: The first four behaviors (grooming, locomotion, feeding, short rest) are mutually exclusive at the level of single events, together defining the wake state of the fly, and collectively complementary to the sleep state.
source: The first four behaviors are mutually exclusive at the level of single events, together defining the wake state of the fly, and collectively complementary to the sleep state (Figure 4A).
evidence: Statement about the relationship between behaviors supported by Figure 4A.

claim: A typical iso31+ fly under 12 hr light:12 hr dark (LD) conditions spent approximately 6% of its daily time grooming, ~24% time locomoting, ~3% time feeding, ~16% resting, and the remaining ~51% sleeping.
source: We found that a typical iso31+ fly under 12 hr light:12 hr dark (LD) conditions spent approximately 6% of its daily time grooming,~24% time locomoting, ~3% time feeding, ~16% resting, and the remaining ~51% sleeping (Figure 4B).
evidence: Statement of behavioral time budget results supported by Figure 4B.

claim: The average iso31+ fly spent ~13% of its awake time grooming.
source: That is, the average iso31+ fly spent ~13% of its awake time grooming.
evidence: Calculation based on the daily time budget data.

claim: Behavioral statistics can vary even between wild-type laboratory strains.
source: It is worth noting here that such behavioral statistics can vary even between wild-type laboratory strains (Colomb and Brembs, 2014; Zalucki et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about strain variability supported by citations.

claim: Canton-S flies groomed ~19% of their awake time.
source: For instance, similar analysis of a Canton-S strain showed that these flies groomed ~19% of their awake time (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statement of behavioral results for Canton-S strain supported by supplementary figure.

claim: The platform for long-term video-tracking and automated analysis can provide a quantitative ethological structure for daily basal fly behavior.
source: These analyses demonstrate that our platform for long-term video-tracking and automated analysis can provide a quantitative ethological structure for daily basal fly behavior.
evidence: Conclusion based on the comprehensive behavioral analysis results.

claim: Flies in the experiments are active for ~34% of the time within a 24 hr period.
source: Flies in our experiments are active for ~34% of the time within a 24 hr period, during which they mostly engage in grooming, locomotion and feeding.
evidence: Statement based on the behavioral time budget data.

claim: Fly grooming behavior is modulated by oscillations of the circadian clock.
source: Behavioral analysis showed that, like sleep, locomotion and feeding, fly grooming behavior is modulated by oscillations of the circadian clock (Figure 5).
evidence: Statement of results from circadian analysis supported by Figure 5.

claim: Kinetics in feeding and locomotion were distinct from those of grooming.
source: However, closer examination revealed that kinetics in feeding and locomotion were distinct from those of grooming (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statement based on kinetic analysis supported by supplementary figure.

claim: Genetic modifications resulted in contrasting changes in grooming, locomotion, and sleep behaviors.
source: Additionally, genetic modifications resulted in contrasting changes in these behaviors (Figure 6).
evidence: Statement of results from genetic experiments supported by Figure 6.

claim: The majority of grooming events detected in the experiments are not triggered by external stimuli such as light, food and locomotor movements.
source: These results together suggest that the majority of grooming events detected in our experiments are not triggered by external stimuli such as light, food and locomotor movements.
evidence: Conclusion based on kinetic and genetic analysis results.

claim: Internal regulatory mechanisms, independent of external stimuli, likely drive programmed grooming behavior.
source: Rather, internal regulatory mechanisms, independent of external stimuli, likely drive this programmed behavior.
evidence: Inference based on the analysis of grooming patterns and their independence from external stimuli.

claim: Multi-day recordings of wild-type flies in constant darkness showed 24 hr rhythms in daily grooming patterns.
source: Multi-day recordings of wild-type flies in constant darkness showed 24 hr rhythms in daily grooming patterns (Figure 5, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statement of results from constant darkness experiments supported by figures.

claim: Grooming rhythms were shifted appropriately in the canonical period mutants perL and perS and abolished in arrhythmic per0 flies.
source: Furthermore, these rhythms were shifted appropriately in the canonical period mutants perL and perS and abolished in arrhythmic per0 flies (Figure 5).
evidence: Statement of results from period mutant experiments supported by Figure 5.

claim: The data support a regulatory model in which timing of programmed grooming behavior is orchestrated by the circadian clock.
source: These data support a regulatory model in which timing of programmed grooming behavior is orchestrated by the circadian clock.
evidence: Conclusion based on the circadian rhythm and period mutant results.

claim: Loss of rhythmicity did not significantly affect the amount of grooming.
source: Notably, since loss of rhythmicity did not significantly affect the amount of grooming (Figure 6A), our results suggest that the primary role of the clock is to organize the behavior in time without influencing the total time flies dedicate to grooming.
evidence: Statement of results from per0 mutant analysis supported by Figure 6A.

claim: The primary role of the clock is to organize grooming behavior in time without influencing the total time flies dedicate to grooming.
source: Notably, since loss of rhythmicity did not significantly affect the amount of grooming (Figure 6A), our results suggest that the primary role of the clock is to organize the behavior in time without influencing the total time flies dedicate to grooming.
evidence: Inference based on the per0 mutant results.

claim: Two circadian mutations, cyc01 and clkJrk, increased the proportion of daily time flies spend grooming.
source: Intriguingly, two other circadian mutations, cyc01 and clkJrk, increased the proportion of daily time flies spend grooming (Figure 6B,C), implying that the changes in grooming level may not be due to circadian defects.
evidence: Statement of results from cyc and clk mutant experiments supported by Figure 6B,C.

claim: The changes in grooming level in cyc01 and clkJrk mutants may not be due to circadian defects.
source: Intriguingly, two other circadian mutations, cyc01 and clkJrk, increased the proportion of daily time flies spend grooming (Figure 6B,C), implying that the changes in grooming level may not be due to circadian defects.
evidence: Inference based on the contrasting effects of per0 vs. cyc01 and clkJrk mutations.

claim: The data are consistent with the hypothesis that clock-independent but cyc- and clk-dependent pathways regulate the amount of programmed grooming behavior.
source: These data are consistent with the hypothesis that clock-independent but cyc- and clk- dependent pathways regulate the amount of programmed grooming behavior.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the differential effects of per0 vs. cyc01 and clkJrk mutations.

claim: Microscopic pathogens can sporulate on the fly cuticle and eventually infect the insect.
source: The present study does not directly address this important question, but given that microscopic pathogens can sporulate on the fly cuticle and eventually infect the insect (St. Leger et al., 2011), persistent grooming may serve as a first line of defense against such attack.
evidence: Statement about pathogen infection supported by citation.

claim: Persistent grooming may serve as a first line of defense against pathogen attack.
source: The present study does not directly address this important question, but given that microscopic pathogens can sporulate on the fly cuticle and eventually infect the insect (St. Leger et al., 2011), persistent grooming may serve as a first line of defense against such attack.
evidence: Speculation based on the potential role of grooming in pathogen defense.

claim: The immune system may constitute another internal program that drives fly grooming.
source: Thus, the immune system may constitute another internal program, similar to the cyc and clk-controlled mechanisms, that drives fly grooming; if so, we hypothesized that mutants with defective immune response may exhibit altered grooming behavior (Lemaitre et al., 1995; Michel et al., 2001).
evidence: Hypothesis about the role of the immune system in grooming, supported by citations.

claim: Grooming was reduced in the immune-deficient imd mutant.
source: Consistent with this, we found that grooming was reduced in the immune-deficient imd mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H), although a second immune-deficient strain lacking a member of the Toll pathway (PGRP-SAseml) did not show a significant change.
evidence: Statement of results from immune mutant experiments supported by supplementary figure.

claim: A second immune-deficient strain lacking a member of the Toll pathway (PGRP-SAseml) did not show a significant change in grooming.
source: Consistent with this, we found that grooming was reduced in the immune-deficient imd mutant (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H), although a second immune-deficient strain lacking a member of the Toll pathway (PGRP-SAseml) did not show a significant change.
evidence: Statement of results from immune mutant experiments supported by supplementary figure.

claim: The data provide strong supporting evidence for programmed grooming in Drosophila.
source: Together, our data provide strong supporting evidence for programmed grooming in Drosophila and suggest that this innate behavior is driven by two possibly distinct sets of regulatory systems.
evidence: Conclusion based on the comprehensive analysis of grooming behavior.

claim: Programmed grooming in Drosophila is driven by two possibly distinct sets of regulatory systems.
source: Together, our data provide strong supporting evidence for programmed grooming in Drosophila and suggest that this innate behavior is driven by two possibly distinct sets of regulatory systems.
evidence: Conclusion based on the differential effects of circadian genes on timing vs. duration of grooming.

claim: The circadian system temporally segregates time-dependent variations in grooming from those of other essential behavioral outputs like feeding and sleep.
source: The circadian system temporally segregates time-dependent variations in grooming from those of other essential behavioral outputs like feeding and sleep.
evidence: Conclusion based on the circadian rhythm analysis of multiple behaviors.

claim: Circadian coordination of grooming underscores a previously under-appreciated importance of this behavior in the daily routine of the fruit fly.
source: Circadian coordination of grooming underscores a previously under-appreciated importance of this behavior in the daily routine of the fruit fly.
evidence: Inference based on the finding that grooming is under circadian control.

claim: The second regulatory system adjusts the level of grooming relative to other behaviors.
source: The second regulatory system adjusts the level of grooming relative to other behaviors.
evidence: Statement about the second regulatory system based on cyc and clk mutant results.

claim: This set of regulation likely confers adaptability on the animal by allowing it to up- or downregulate grooming as necessitated by internal and external conditions.
source: This set of regulation likely confers adaptability on the animal by allowing it to up- or downregulate grooming as necessitated by internal and external conditions.
evidence: Speculation about the functional significance of the second regulatory system.

claim: The dual control mechanism of grooming is highly reminiscent of the two-process framework---circadian and homeostatic---that is widely used in understanding sleep regulation.
source: The dual control mechanism of grooming proposed here is highly reminiscent of the two-process framework---circadian and homeostatic---that is widely used in understanding sleep regulation (Borbély, 1982).
evidence: Comparison to the established two-process model of sleep regulation, supported by citation.

claim: This work has not demonstrated grooming is under homeostatic control.
source: Although this work has not demonstrated grooming is under homeostatic control, future studies could be aimed at better characterizing the nature of the non-circadian regulatory system of fly grooming.
evidence: Acknowledgment of a limitation of the current study.

claim: The apparatus can be assembled easily, and the accompanying analytics are available publicly.
source: The apparatus can be assembled easily, and the accompanying analytics are available publicly.
evidence: Statement about the accessibility of the methods.

claim: The platform can detect innate grooming behavior simultaneously and for days at a time in multiple individual fruit flies.
source: In summary, we present here a new platform to detect innate grooming behavior simultaneously and for days at a time in multiple individual fruit flies.
evidence: Summary statement about the capabilities of the platform.

claim: Szebenyi delineated all the major modes of fly grooming and suggested that repetitive grooming actions may closely follow a preset sequence.
source: Szebenyi delineated all the major modes of fly grooming and suggested that repetitive grooming actions may closely follow a preset sequence (Szebenyi, 1969).
evidence: Statement about historical research supported by citation.

claim: A subsequent study in the blowfly offered a more refined mechanistic picture of insect grooming by proposing that the sequential actions form a hierarchical structure.
source: A subsequent study in the blowfly offered a more refined mechanistic picture of insect grooming by proposing that the sequential actions form a hierarchical structure (Dawkins and Dawkins, 1976).
evidence: Statement about historical research supported by citation.

claim: An elegant study in Drosophila recently confirmed that grooming actions form a hierarchical structure.
source: Combining modern computational and genetic tools, an elegant study in Drosophila recently confirmed these previous hypotheses (Seeds et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about recent research supported by citation.

claim: Fruit flies may groom spontaneously in the absence of any apparent stimulus.
source: That fruit flies may groom spontaneously in the absence of any apparent stimulus has also been previously suggested (Connolly, 1968; Tinbergen, 1965).
evidence: Statement about historical observations supported by citations.

claim: Over a period of hours, grooming is temporally structured by the fly circadian clock, with peak activity around dawn and dusk.
source: Consistent with this, our work provides evidence that fruit flies groom as part of their daily repertoire of internally programmed behaviors and often without any obvious external stimulus. Our analysis revealed that over a period of hours, grooming is temporally structured by the fly circadian clock, with peak activity around dawn and dusk.
evidence: Statement of results from the circadian analysis.

claim: The study identifies transcription factors CLOCK and CYCLE as critical molecular components that control the amplitude of programmed Drosophila grooming.
source: The study also identifies transcription factors CLOCK and CYCLE as critical molecular components that control the amplitude of programmed Drosophila grooming.
evidence: Statement of results from genetic experiments.

claim: Machine-learning is increasingly gaining popularity due to its applicability to virtually any problem involving pattern classification, including in studies aimed at deconstructing stereotyped behavior in the fruit fly.
source: Machine-learning is increasingly gaining popularity due to its applicability to virtually any problem involving pattern classification, including in studies aimed at deconstructing stereotyped behavior in the fruit fly (Branson et al., 2009; Kabra et al., 2013; Kain et al., 2013; Mendes et al., 2013; Valletta et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about the trend in the field supported by citations.

claim: The approach relies on a supervised k-nearest neighbors algorithm to broadly classify behavior into grooming, locomotion and rest.
source: Our approach relies, in particular, on a supervised k-nearest neighbors algorithm to broadly classify behavior into grooming, locomotion and rest (Figure 2).
evidence: Direct description of the algorithmic approach.

claim: Previous methods offer important details on different modes of grooming, leg movements, and fly-fly interactions from short videos.
source: While previous methods offer important details on different modes of grooming (Berman et al., 2014; Seeds et al., 2014), leg movements (Kain et al., 2013; Mendes et al., 2013), and fly-fly interactions (Branson et al., 2009; Kabra et al., 2013) from short videos, the methods have limited capability for interpreting multi-day and multi-fly recordings.
evidence: Statement about the capabilities of previous methods supported by citations.

claim: Previous methods have limited capability for interpreting multi-day and multi-fly recordings.
source: While previous methods offer important details on different modes of grooming (Berman et al., 2014; Seeds et al., 2014), leg movements (Kain et al., 2013; Mendes et al., 2013), and fly-fly interactions (Branson et al., 2009; Kabra et al., 2013) from short videos, the methods have limited capability for interpreting multi-day and multi-fly recordings.
evidence: Statement about the limitations of previous methods.

claim: The method presented here offers less detail on modes of grooming, but can instead readily dissect circadian time-scale recordings into three to five behavioral classes on a typical personal computer.
source: The method presented here offers less detail on modes of grooming, but can instead readily dissect circadian time-scale recordings into three to five behavioral classes on a typical personal computer.
evidence: Statement about the trade-offs and capabilities of the current method.

claim: Most items used in the apparatus are standard in a typical circadian experiment studying fly locomotion or sleep using the Drosophila Activity Monitor (DAM).
source: First, most items used in the apparatus, including the ~6 cm tubes in which flies are visualized, are standard in a typical circadian experiment studying fly locomotion or sleep (Lazopulo et al., 2015; Pfeiffenberger et al., 2010) using the Drosophila Activity Monitor (DAM).
evidence: Statement about the compatibility with existing equipment supported by citations.

claim: The retention of the basic design should lower the technical hurdle for the interested investigator who is likely to be one already engaged in locomotion and sleep studies in Drosophila.
source: The retention of this basic feature should lower the technical hurdle for the interested investigator who is likely to be one already engaged in locomotion and sleep studies in Drosophila.
evidence: Inference about the accessibility of the method.

claim: The use of a shared design to house flies means that both experimental subjects and certain conclusions drawn from one platform may be readily transferred to the other.
source: The use of a shared design to house flies also means that both experimental subjects and certain conclusions drawn from one platform may be readily transferred to the other.
evidence: Inference about the benefits of using a standardized design.

claim: Most current grooming methods require specialized equipment for fly stimulation and detection, elaborate optics, or a specific form of fluorescence microscopy.
source: Most current grooming methods require specialized equipment for fly stimulation and detection (Seeds et al., 2014), elaborate optics (Kain et al., 2013), or a specific form of fluorescence microscopy (Mendes et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about the requirements of current methods supported by citations.

claim: The apparatus can simultaneously monitor up to ~20 flies.
source: Second, our apparatus can simultaneously monitor up to ~20 flies, while the existing approaches, although offering higher-resolution data, monitor only one animal at a time.
evidence: Direct statement about the throughput capability of the apparatus.

claim: Existing approaches, although offering higher-resolution data, monitor only one animal at a time.
source: Second, our apparatus can simultaneously monitor up to ~20 flies, while the existing approaches, although offering higher-resolution data, monitor only one animal at a time.
evidence: Statement about the limitations of existing approaches.

claim: The scalability and high-throughput nature of the platform should appeal to investigators interested in large-scale genetic studies.
source: The scalability and high-throughput nature of our platform should appeal to investigators interested in, for example, large-scale genetic studies to identify mechanisms that differentially affect grooming, locomotion and rest (King et al., 2016).
evidence: Inference about the potential applications of the platform.

claim: The flies in the apparatus are allowed to move freely over a distance roughly 10 times their body length and still remain in the camera's field of view.
source: Finally, the flies in our apparatus are allowed to move freely over a distance roughly 10 times their body length and still remain in the camera's field of view while technical constraints in other studies limit visualization to short distances (Mendes et al., 2013).
evidence: Direct statement about the mobility allowed in the apparatus.

claim: Technical constraints in other studies limit visualization to short distances.
source: Finally, the flies in our apparatus are allowed to move freely over a distance roughly 10 times their body length and still remain in the camera's field of view while technical constraints in other studies limit visualization to short distances (Mendes et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about the limitations of other studies supported by citation.

claim: The relative freedom of mobility, access to food, and long time-scales of observation offered by the apparatus facilitate analysis of basal, internally programmed behavior.
source: The relative freedom of mobility, access to food, and long time-scales of observation offered by our apparatus thus facilitate analysis of basal, internally programmed behavior.
evidence: Inference about the advantages of the apparatus for studying programmed behavior.

claim: Flies consistently devote a significant fraction of time to grooming behavior during periods of wakefulness (13%).
source: First, we found that flies consistently devote a significant fraction of time to grooming behavior during periods of wakefulness (13%), and surprisingly, that grooming behavior is observed even during periods of reduced locomotor activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Statement of results from behavioral analysis supported by supplementary figure.

claim: Grooming behavior is observed even during periods of reduced locomotor activity.
source: First, we found that flies consistently devote a significant fraction of time to grooming behavior during periods of wakefulness (13%), and surprisingly, that grooming behavior is observed even during periods of reduced locomotor activity (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Statement of results from behavioral analysis supported by supplementary figure.

claim: The benefits of grooming outweigh the caloric resources expended and the resulting interruption of rest.
source: This suggests that the benefits of grooming outweigh the caloric resources expended and the resulting interruption of rest, underscoring the hypothesis that daily grooming is a fundamental behavior of Drosophila.
evidence: Inference based on the significant time flies spend grooming.

claim: Daily grooming is a fundamental behavior of Drosophila.
source: This suggests that the benefits of grooming outweigh the caloric resources expended and the resulting interruption of rest, underscoring the hypothesis that daily grooming is a fundamental behavior of Drosophila.
evidence: Hypothesis based on the significant time flies spend grooming.

claim: A few recent studies have shown that fly grooming can be directly induced by peripheral stimuli.
source: A few recent studies (Hampel et al., 2015; Phillis et al., 1993; Seeds et al., 2014) have shown that fly grooming can be directly induced by peripheral stimuli, and there has been considerable progress toward identifying the behavioral and neural aspects of such stimulus-induced grooming.
evidence: Statement about recent research supported by citations.

claim: There has been considerable progress toward identifying the behavioral and neural aspects of stimulus-induced grooming.
source: A few recent studies (Hampel et al., 2015; Phillis et al., 1993; Seeds et al., 2014) have shown that fly grooming can be directly induced by peripheral stimuli, and there has been considerable progress toward identifying the behavioral and neural aspects of such stimulus-induced grooming.
evidence: Statement about recent progress supported by citations.

claim: Programmed grooming, or grooming in the absence of a macroscopic stimulus, remains relatively understudied in Drosophila.
source: However, programmed grooming, or grooming in the absence of a macroscopic stimulus, remains relatively understudied in Drosophila.
evidence: Statement about the current state of research in the field.

claim: The existence of programmed grooming, first proposed in the mid 60s, still remains unreported.
source: To our knowledge, the existence of programmed grooming, first proposed in the mid 60s, still remains unreported.
evidence: Statement about the gap in the literature.

claim: Data from this study suggest that a significant portion of daily fly grooming is driven by internal programs.
source: Data from this study suggest that a significant portion of daily fly grooming is driven by internal programs.
evidence: Conclusion based on the comprehensive analysis of grooming behavior.

claim: Environmental light-dark cycles through influence on the circadian clock are known to drive rhythmic changes in fly sleep and wake durations and within the awake state, feeding, and locomotor activities.
source: Indeed, environmental light-dark cycles through influence on the circadian clock are known to drive rhythmic changes in fly sleep and wake durations and within the awake state, feeding, and locomotor activities (Chatterjee and Rouyer, 2016; Pfeiffenberger et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement about established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: That rhythms persist in the absence of LD cycles is generally considered to be strong support for clock control of behaviors.
source: That these rhythms persisted in the absence of LD cycles is generally considered to be strong support for clock control of these behaviors.
evidence: Statement about the interpretation of circadian rhythm data, representing established knowledge.

claim: The mutual exclusivity of behaviors seen at the level of individual events did not persist at the level of fractional time in each behavior where the long timescale modulations are visible.
source: We recognized that the mutual exclusivity of the behaviors seen at the level of individual events (Figure 4A) did not persist at the level of fractional time in each behavior where the long timescale modulations are visible (Figure 4E).
evidence: Statement about the data representation supported by figures.

claim: In the fractional time representation, rhythmicity of one behavior (i.e. grooming) did not dictate rhythmic status of another (i.e. locomotion).
source: In this representation, therefore, rhythmicity of one behavior (i.e. grooming) did not dictate rhythmic status of another (i.e. locomotion).
evidence: Inference based on the properties of the binned data representation.

claim: Rhythmicity in locomotion and wakefulness were intact regardless of the rhythmic status of grooming in the shuffling experiments.
source: In either case, we found that rhythmicity in locomotion and wakefulness were intact regardless of the rhythmic status of grooming.
evidence: Statement of results from the shuffling simulation experiments.

claim: The simulation result suggested that circadian control of fly locomotion and wakefulness does not guarantee circadian control of underlying basal grooming.
source: The simulation result suggested that circadian control of fly locomotion and wakefulness does not guarantee circadian control of underlying basal grooming, at least as measured from changes in the duration of the behaviors.
evidence: Conclusion based on the shuffling simulation results.

claim: Demonstration of robust ~24 hr rhythms in grooming in the absence of any external cues should be strong evidence in favor of circadian control of the behavior.
source: Therefore, demonstration of robust ~24 hr rhythms in grooming in the absence of any external cues should be strong evidence in favor of circadian control of the behavior.
evidence: Statement about the interpretation of circadian rhythm data.

claim: In the absence of light cues, locomotor, feeding and sleep showed the familiar clock-driven rhythms in their daily timing.
source: In the absence of light cues, locomotor, feeding and sleep showed the familiar clock-driven rhythms in their daily timing (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: Statement of results from constant darkness experiments supported by Figure 5A,B.

claim: Short rest appeared to undergo rhythmic changes but spectral analysis indicated these changes did not result in statistically significant rhythms at the p=0.05 level.
source: Although short rest appeared to undergo rhythmic changes (Figure 5A), spectral analysis indicated these changes did not result in statistically significant rhythms at the p=0.05 level (Figure 5B).
evidence: Statement of results from spectral analysis supported by Figure 5A,B.

claim: Lack of rhythms in short rest is consistent with the reasoning that rhythmic wakefulness and locomotion does not necessarily imply rhythmicity of each behavior in the awake state.
source: Lack of rhythms in short rest is consistent with our earlier reasoning that rhythmic wakefulness and locomotion does not necessarily imply rhythmicity of each behavior in the awake state.
evidence: Inference connecting the short rest results to the earlier simulation results.

claim: Grooming data showed periodic changes in constant darkness.
source: Grooming data also showed periodic changes in constant darkness (Figure 5C).
evidence: Statement of results from constant darkness experiments supported by Figure 5C.

claim: Power spectra of individual time-series indicated periodic changes in grooming to be statistically rhythmic by revealing peaks significant at p=0.01 in 100% of flies (29 out of 29 individuals).
source: Power spectra of individual time-series ('WT' in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A) indicated these periodic changes to be statistically rhythmic by revealing peaks significant at p=0.01 in 100% of flies (29 out of 29 individuals, Figure 5E).
evidence: Statement of results from spectral analysis supported by figures.

claim: The average period of grooming oscillations was 23.72 hr, with a standard deviation of 0.72 hr.
source: The average period of oscillations was 23.72 hr, with a standard deviation of 0.72 hr (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Statement of results from period analysis supported by supplementary figure.

claim: The presence of robust circadian rhythms in grooming in the absence of external cues further support the hypothesis that fly basal grooming is under control of the internal timekeeper.
source: The presence of these robust circadian rhythms in the absence of external cues further support the hypothesis that fly basal grooming is under control of the internal timekeeper.
evidence: Conclusion based on the constant darkness grooming rhythm results.

claim: Knowing locomotion or wakefulness is rhythmic did not inform about the rhythmic status of grooming.
source: Consistent with our prediction that grooming rhythms in DD do not necessarily follow from rhythms in locomotion or wakefulness, we found that knowing locomotion or wakefulness is rhythmic did not inform about the rhythmic status of grooming (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Statement of results from additional shuffling experiments supported by supplementary figure.

claim: The simulation results do not demonstrate bidirectional independence of rhythmicity in wakefulness and grooming but, only that rhythmicity of wakefulness does not depend on that of grooming.
source: It should be noted here that our simulation results do not demonstrate bidirectional independence of rhythmicity in wakefulness and grooming but, only that rhythmicity of wakefulness does not depend on that of grooming.
evidence: Clarification about the interpretation of the simulation results.

claim: Demonstration of fully independent rhythms in wakefulness and grooming is beyond the scope of the present study.
source: Demonstration of fully independent rhythms in the two behaviors is beyond the scope of the present study.
evidence: Statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: The Drosophila clock is composed of two interlocked genetic feedback loops in which period (per) is one of the core components and whose transcription is controlled by the primary transcription factors Clock (clk) and Cycle (cyc).
source: The Drosophila clock is composed of two interlocked genetic feedback loops in which period (per) is one of the core components and whose transcription is controlled by the primary transcription factors Clock (clk) and Cycle (cyc) (Allada and Chung, 2010).
evidence: Statement about the molecular basis of the circadian clock supported by citation.

claim: The per gene has several well-characterized mutant alleles, two of which---perS and perL---produce short and long circadian rhythms, respectively, while a third, per0, results in arrhythmic behavior.
source: The per gene has several well-characterized mutant alleles, two of which---perS and perL---produce short and long circadian rhythms, respectively, while a third, per0, results in arrhythmic behavior (Konopka and Benzer, 1971).
evidence: Statement about period mutants supported by citation.

claim: The periods of oscillation in grooming were well within published values of circadian rhythms of perS and perL mutants.
source: The periods of oscillation in grooming were well within published values of circadian rhythms of these mutants (Konopka and Benzer, 1971) and in agreement with alterations in locomotor rhythms of the flies (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Statement comparing results to published values, supported by citation and supplementary figure.

claim: Grooming in per0 flies was arrhythmic.
source: Consistent with these results, grooming in per0 flies was arrhythmic (Figure 5C, bottom row) and, when analyzed at the individual fly level, the power spectra unveiled the absence of statistically significant rhythms in 19 out of 20 flies at p=0.01 level (Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statement of results from per0 mutant experiments supported by figures.

claim: Analysis of grooming patterns in cyc01 and clkJrk, arrhythmic mutants of cyc and clk, also showed loss of circadian rhythms.
source: Moreover, analysis of grooming patterns in cyc01 (Rutila et al., 1998) and clkJrk (Allada et al., 1998), arrhythmic mutants of cyc and clk, also showed loss of circadian rhythms (Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 3B–D).
evidence: Statement of results from cyc and clk mutant experiments supported by figures and citations.

claim: The results support the hypothesis that the circadian clock temporally modulates fly grooming.
source: Together, these results support the hypothesis that the circadian clock temporally modulates fly grooming.
evidence: Conclusion based on the circadian mutant results.

claim: Despite causing major changes in temporal patterns of grooming, the per0 mutation did not significantly change the average duration of grooming in these flies.
source: Despite causing major changes in temporal patterns of grooming, the per0 mutation did not significantly change the average duration of grooming in these flies (Figure 6A).
evidence: Statement of results from per0 mutant analysis supported by Figure 6A.

claim: cyc01 and clkJrk mutants both exhibited increased daily average grooming relative to their respective genetic controls.
source: In contrast, cyc01 and clkJrk mutants both exhibited increased daily average grooming relative to their respective genetic controls (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Statement of results from cyc and clk mutant experiments supported by Figure 6B,C.

claim: While both cyc01 and clkJrk mutants exhibited increased grooming duration, this change was accompanied by opposing changes in their locomotion.
source: While both mutants exhibited increased grooming duration, this change was accompanied by opposing changes in their locomotion: cyc01 flies spent less time and clkJrk flies spent almost twice as much time in locomotion (Figure 6B,C, pie plots).
evidence: Statement of results from cyc and clk mutant experiments supported by Figure 6B,C.

claim: The increase in cyc01 grooming came almost entirely from loss of locomotor activity while the increase in clkJrk grooming came from loss of sleep.
source: Thus, the increase in cyc01 grooming came almost entirely from loss of locomotor activity while the increase in clkJrk grooming came from loss of sleep.
evidence: Inference based on the behavioral time budget changes in cyc01 and clkJrk mutants.

claim: The results support the hypothesis that locomotion and grooming are partly independent behaviors.
source: These results support the hypothesis that locomotion and grooming are partly independent behaviors and further suggests that the cyc01 and clkJrk mutations alter the insect's internal homeostasis in distinct ways, similar to phenotypic differences reported previously in sleep studies involving cyc01 and clkJrk (Hendricks et al., 2003; Shaw et al., 2002).
evidence: Conclusion based on the contrasting effects of cyc01 and clkJrk mutations, supported by citations.

claim: The cyc01 and clkJrk mutations alter the insect's internal homeostasis in distinct ways, similar to phenotypic differences reported previously in sleep studies.
source: These results support the hypothesis that locomotion and grooming are partly independent behaviors and further suggests that the cyc01 and clkJrk mutations alter the insect's internal homeostasis in distinct ways, similar to phenotypic differences reported previously in sleep studies involving cyc01 and clkJrk (Hendricks et al., 2003; Shaw et al., 2002).
evidence: Inference based on the contrasting effects of cyc01 and clkJrk mutations, supported by citations to sleep studies.

claim: Together with per0 data, the results raise the possibility of non-circadian roles for cyc and clk in setting the duration of internally driven grooming in Drosophila.
source: Importantly, together with per0 data, the results raise the possibility of non-circadian roles for cyc and clk in setting the duration of internally driven grooming in Drosophila.
evidence: Conclusion based on the differential effects of per0 vs. cyc01 and clkJrk mutations.

claim: cycle and clock have been implicated in stress response, particularly in regulating level of sleep in response to sleep deprivation and adjusting locomotor output in response to nutrient unavailability.
source: cycle and clock have also been implicated in stress response, particularly in regulating level of sleep in response to sleep deprivation and adjusting locomotor output in response to nutrient unavailability (Hendricks et al., 2003; Keene et al., 2010; Shaw et al., 2002).
evidence: Statement about the roles of cyc and clk supported by citations.

claim: Grooming and sleep have both been previously linked to stress.
source: Because grooming and sleep have both been previously linked to stress, we asked whether reduction in sleep is always accompanied by an increase in grooming as seen in our clkJrk data.
evidence: Statement about the relationship between grooming, sleep, and stress, representing established knowledge.

claim: Both fumin and sleepless (sss) strains have extremely low levels of sleep.
source: Consistent with the original studies (Koh et al., 2008; Kume et al., 2005), our method found both strains to have extremely low levels of sleep (Figure 6D,E, pie plots).
evidence: Statement of results from sleep mutant experiments supported by Figure 6D,E and citations.

claim: Loss of sleep in fumin was accompanied by an upregulation in grooming.
source: But, while loss of sleep in fumin was accompanied by an upregulation in grooming (Figure 6D), loss of sleep in sss was accompanied by a dramatic downregulation in grooming, compared to control flies (Figure 6E).
evidence: Statement of results from fumin mutant experiments supported by Figure 6D.

claim: Loss of sleep in sss was accompanied by a dramatic downregulation in grooming, compared to control flies.
source: But, while loss of sleep in fumin was accompanied by an upregulation in grooming (Figure 6D), loss of sleep in sss was accompanied by a dramatic downregulation in grooming, compared to control flies (Figure 6E).
evidence: Statement of results from sss mutant experiments supported by Figure 6E.

claim: Divergent relationships exist between sleep and grooming (e.g. sss vs. fumin) and between locomotion and grooming (e.g. clkJrk vs. cyc01).
source: These divergent relationships between sleep and grooming (e.g. sss vs. fumin) and between locomotion and grooming (e.g. clkJrk vs. cyc01) became more evident when individuals of different genotypes were compared together (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F,G).
evidence: Statement about the divergent relationships supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Resetting of the level of internally-driven grooming can occur via a number of ways with complex compensatory changes in sleep and locomotor behavior.
source: These results suggest that resetting of the level of internally-driven grooming can occur via a number of ways with complex compensatory changes in sleep and locomotor behavior.
evidence: Conclusion based on the diverse effects of different mutations on grooming and other behaviors.

claim: Accumulated data suggest that grooming is an innate fly behavior controlled by two major regulators.
source: Accumulated data from our experiments suggest that grooming is an innate fly behavior controlled by two major regulators.
evidence: Summary conclusion based on all the experimental results.

claim: One regulator controls temporal patterns in grooming and the other controls amount of time spent in grooming.
source: One of these regulators controls temporal patterns in grooming and the other controls amount of time spent in grooming.
evidence: Summary of the dual control model based on experimental results.

claim: Circadian genes per, cyc and clk are involved in controlling the timing of peaks/troughs in grooming rhythms.
source: Circadian genes per, cyc and clk are involved in controlling the timing of peaks/troughs in grooming rhythms while cyc and clk are also involved in setting how much time is spent grooming.
evidence: Summary of the roles of circadian genes based on experimental results.

claim: cyc and clk are also involved in setting how much time is spent grooming.
source: Circadian genes per, cyc and clk are involved in controlling the timing of peaks/troughs in grooming rhythms while cyc and clk are also involved in setting how much time is spent grooming.
evidence: Summary of the roles of cyc and clk based on experimental results.

claim: The apparent absence of per from the second regulatory mechanism is consistent with the possibility that the two control mechanisms operate independently.
source: The apparent absence of per from the second regulatory mechanism is consistent with the possibility that the two control mechanisms operate independently.
evidence: Inference based on the differential effects of per0 vs. cyc01 and clkJrk mutations.

claim: Nearly all animals tested exhibit daily basal grooming behavior.
source: Nearly all animals tested exhibit daily basal grooming behavior, suggesting that grooming is not only fundamental to health but also reflects a generally healthy state.
evidence: Statement about the universality of grooming behavior, representing established knowledge.

claim: Grooming is not only fundamental to health but also reflects a generally healthy state.
source: Nearly all animals tested exhibit daily basal grooming behavior, suggesting that grooming is not only fundamental to health but also reflects a generally healthy state.
evidence: Inference based on the universality of grooming behavior.

claim: Loss of grooming is indicative of sickness behavior associated with infection or old age, and, in the case of humans, mental illness.
source: Consistent with this, loss of grooming is indicative of sickness behavior (Hart, 1988) associated with infection or old age, and, in the case of humans, mental illness.
evidence: Statement about the significance of grooming loss supported by citation.

claim: A greater understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating grooming would provide insight into the principles and neural circuits underlying other complex programmed behaviors.
source: A greater understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating grooming would provide insight into the principles and neural circuits underlying other complex programmed behaviors, as well as potentially identify biomarkers of pathological disease states.
evidence: Speculation about the potential benefits of studying grooming mechanisms.

claim: Understanding grooming mechanisms could potentially identify biomarkers of pathological disease states.
source: A greater understanding of the molecular mechanisms regulating grooming would provide insight into the principles and neural circuits underlying other complex programmed behaviors, as well as potentially identify biomarkers of pathological disease states.
evidence: Speculation about the potential applications of grooming research.

claim: The development of the platform will facilitate high-throughput and unbiased analysis of the genetic regulators and neural circuits that control grooming.
source: The development of our platform will facilitate high-throughput and unbiased analysis of the genetic regulators and neural circuits that control grooming, as well as those responsible for loss of grooming in the context of disease.
evidence: Statement about the potential applications of the platform.

claim: The platform will facilitate analysis of genetic regulators and neural circuits responsible for loss of grooming in the context of disease.
source: The development of our platform will facilitate high-throughput and unbiased analysis of the genetic regulators and neural circuits that control grooming, as well as those responsible for loss of grooming in the context of disease.
evidence: Statement about the potential applications of the platform.

claim: Using a desktop computer with Intel Core i7-4770 3.4 GHz processer and 4 × 4 G DDR3 1600 MHz RAM, it takes ~7 hr to extract grooming, locomotion and rest data from an 8 hr video of 20 flies recorded in 10 Hz at 1280 pixel ×960 pixel resolution.
source: Using a desktop computer with Intel Core i7-4770 3.4 GHz processer and 4 × 4 G DDR3 1600 MHz RAM, it takes ~7 hr to extract grooming, locomotion and rest data from an 8 hr video of 20 flies recorded in 10 Hz (in total 288,000 frames) at 1280 pixel ×960 pixel resolution.
evidence: Direct statement about the computational requirements and processing time.

claim: Videos are analyzed every two frames (5 Hz), which is sufficient to capture grooming events.
source: Videos are analyzed every two frames (5 Hz), which is sufficient to capture grooming events.
evidence: Statement about the analysis frame rate and its sufficiency.

claim: A C0 = 10 excludes 99.99% of noise-related changes in grayscale values.
source: Based on this distribution, we set C0=10, which excludes 99.99% of noise-related changes in grayscale values.
evidence: Statement about the effectiveness of the threshold based on noise analysis.

claim: All experiments were done with 5–8 days old males at 260C and 70–80% relative humidity in a custom-built behavior tracking chamber.
source: All experiments were done with 5–8 days old males at 260C and 70–80% relative humidity in a custom-built behavior tracking chamber (Figure 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Direct description of the experimental conditions.
